does: Dusts a piece of food, often after it has been marinated, in a thin layer of potato starch or cornstarch just before frying. It fries to a crisp, light, pale crust.

intro.what: Food receives a thin dry starch coating immediately before frying.
intro.why: The amount and timing of coating matter: loose starch or absorbed moisture can turn a light crust heavy and gluey.

how: Pat the food dry and shake off any marinade that is dripping.
Tip the starch into a tray and turn each piece in it, pressing lightly.
Tap off the loose starch, as too much turns pasty in the oil.
Fry straight away, before the starch dampens and turns gluey.

cues.text: The coating is thin, dry and even, with no wet spots.
The piece crackles in the oil.

mistakes.mistake: Coating too thickly, which turns gluey and heavy.
Coating long before frying, so that the starch gets wet.

quiz.question: What crust is this coating intended to produce?
quiz.because: A thin starch film fries differently from a heavy damp coating.

quiz.question: What should happen after turning the food in starch?
choices: Tap away loose starch and fry promptly.
Pile on more starch and leave it standing.
Soak the coated food before frying.
quiz.because: Removing excess and frying promptly help keep the coating thin and dry.

quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended coating?
choices: Thin, dry and even without wet patches.
A glossy paste sliding off the food.
quiz.because: A dry even film shows the starch has not become a heavy wet layer.

quiz.question: The starch turned wet while waiting. What should change?
choices: Coat earlier so it absorbs more moisture.
Leave the pieces pressed together after coating.
quiz.because: Moisture reaches the starch as it waits, so timing the coating near frying preserves its texture.

variant_of.differs: The coat is starch, not flour, so it fries thinner, crisper and paler.
